utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, case number IT-95-16-T,the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. We regret this delay. It's not our fault. I think we may continue with the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning witness, my name is Franck Terrier. I'm one of the Prosecution members. I would like to put a few questions to you following your testimony. I believe you have an exact memory of what you stated when you were testifying and the questions that were put to you. These are some questions which I'm going to come back to myself. During the course of your testimony you said that you knew two of the accused, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. I would like now to ask you to tell this Tribunal whether you know well or less well the other accused in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know (sic) that I didn't know the Kupreskics well. I said that I knew Zoran Kupreskic well, better than Mirjan though. As for the rest, I know some better, others less. Others I know only by sight, I didn't really contact them, but this is a small town and everybody knows one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, would you please state more precisely which of the accused you knew at that time, the at the time of the events, that is to say 1993, 1992.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan, Vlatko, Vlado and from sight I knew Papic. I did not know Mr. Josipovic until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. During the course of your testimony, you brought up another -- a number of issues which are military in nature. You gave your point of views and you gave your technical -- your point on a number of questions. I would like to know exactly what kind of military training you received.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said, in 1977 I left the army, having completed reserve officer training. So I left the army as a reserve lieutenant. I assumed certain duties in the Territorial Defence of the municipality of the Vitez, and I was engaged in various courses. During those years before the war, I spent over 120 days training, and that is part of my military record, and the last course I did was at a military centre in Pazarici where I was trained to be a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You stated, witness, that you joined the Territorial Defence in 1972 as a non-commissioned officer in the reserves. I would like for you to make a few comments about what happened at that time, until the beginning of the war. What were the members of the Territorial Defence -- what were its members, and what kind of training did these men received who were part of these units, what their status is and what kind of weaponry did they use?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Many questions in one question, so let us tackle them one at a time. I'm not talking about '87, I'm talking about '77, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: '77, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I received '87 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, we agree, it is 1977, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the establishment of the TO at that time was a modification of the setup of the Yugoslav People's Army at that time. That is to say, the municipal of the TO of Vitez was formed along similar lines to those in the active units of the Yugoslav People's Army. That is to say that we had a staff command that worked either in peacetime conditions or in wartime conditions. In peacetime conditions, the head of the staff and some officers in the staff were professional officers, the rest belonged to the reserve corps. In case of immediate threat of war, the peacetime function of the staff grew into a wartime function of the staff. That is to say that the head of staff of the Territorial Defence became the head of the command, and the other head of staff was recruited from the reserve corps, naturally. There were other posts from the reserve corps. For example, the head for the PNHBO. Then the Operations Officer was a professional, the officer for establishment was a professional. However, as records this other part, the basic unit in the TO was Territorial Defence detachment. That would have been a battalion, a reinforced battalion. Then there was the staff and the units attached to the staff. This functioned in accordance with the regulations of the Yugoslav People's Army. That is to say, the TO was one form of organisation of the army of Yugoslavia. There was an active component, and this other component which was practically the passive reserve component, that was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did the fact of participating in the Territorial Defence before the war -- all this, of course, is before the war in the former Yugoslavia. Did the fact of participating as a member of these units, was this done on a voluntary basis by the citizens?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: After doing one's active military service, at that time every citizen of our country was duty-bound to be organised in some form of defence as called upon. So it was my duty, as well as that of others, to be at the Territorial Defence at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So the -- to participate in the Territorial Defence was an occupation of all citizens, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not for all citizens. It was not an obligation for all citizens. Not all were organised within the TO, the Territorial Defence. There were persons who belonged to the TO and who held certain posts in the TO, but not everyone. Some people were in the Civil Defence, others belonged to units at their place of work, et cetera. So this was as called upon. This is not something that one did of one's own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We understand each other. I would like to recall your position so there's no ambiguity. In the former Yugoslavia, all citizens who participated in the defence as reservists, at least as reservists, was an obligation of all citizens?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: When being called up to do so or called upon to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When called upon to do so, I understand. Was the Territorial Defence organised, as you described, you described a part of its organisation, but was there a territorial base to this as well?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. From the point of view of territory we were assigned to the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As part of the municipality of Vitez, were the units of the Territorial Defence in the villages?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: If there were units in villages this was not according to formations, official formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please explain what a unit stationed in a village, which is a member of the Territorial Defence, would you please specify exactly what you mean by your response?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with military regulations. This can even go beyond the establishment of the Territorial Defence and regulations, because I said what the units and formations of Territorial Defence were like a few minutes ago. Territorial Defence does not have village units as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What training was given to citizens within the former Yugoslavia, of course, when they were called upon, within the context of defence?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Are we talking about units of Territorial Defence are or we talking about citizens in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's talk about citizens in general, who, once called upon, as you stated, would be duty-bound to participate in the defence of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can tell you about training in Territorial Defence units, and that is such a broad concept that I cannot go into now. However, when speaking about TO units, I can say that after doing one's military service, every year a plan for the training of units was adopted for the following year. So certain units had some kind of training in these various teaching centres every two years or every five years. That is to say, squads, platoons, companies, et cetera. The larger units were called up on rare occasions, because that was expensive, whereas the smaller units were called up every two years. It all depended on the plan that was adopted during the previous year. So sometime in October, roughly, the programme of training for the following year would be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Consequently then, can we say that in the former Yugoslavia, in Yugoslavia before the war, as in other countries in Europe, all citizens, on a regular basis, would receive military training?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to respond to all these questions related to citizens all the time, you know. I cannot talk about citizens. I can talk about units within the Territorial Defence, you know. And that does not include all citizens, it includes only part of the people who were organised in the Territorial Defence, and you know, as well as I do, approximately what number of people were involved. It certainly does not speak of the entire citizenry of the municipality of Vitez. I can only speak, as I said -- I can only speak about the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm calling upon your competence in military affairs and in the Territorial Defence as well, but what I'm interested in right now is in the formal system of defence in the former Yugoslavia, which may also involve other units and other means of action than strictly the Territorial Defence which you spoke about, would also interest me is the role of a citizen. I hope this word does not bother you. I'm looking to see what the participation of the citizens in the former Yugoslavia was. That is the nature of the question I'm asking you. If you wish to take a moment, that is fine. Let us look at what happened with the citizens in the former Yugoslavia, and let's talk about, in particular, for the interests of this Tribunal and for us all, what type of training, in view of a -- the eventual or possible conflict, each citizen received.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not clear to me how you came to this conclusion that I was an expert in defence and in terms of the participation of the entire population. I spoke explicitly in my statement of the Territorial Defence, and I said that I was in the TO. And may I say straightaway that there weren't any experts of this nature who were -- people who were aware of the entire -- the general picture. We all had our respective lines of work. I can talk to you about the TO, but I cannot talk to you about the structure of defence of the country at large because I'm not competent to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, I would like to go on to another subject dealing with the spring of 1992. Would you please explain how the defence of Bosnia, the area in which you were living, was defended against the Serb Nation? That is to say, from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know -- well, at that time I was not part of the military organisation. I was attached to the TO, but I was at home and I was waiting to see what would happen and whether they would call me up. And I was following the media, of course, and the situation in that part of the world. I realised that this attack on Slovenia, Croatia and on Bosnia-Herzegovina too by the Serb aggressors, that the Croatian people tried to organise themselves to defend these areas. I think that this was an organisation based on self-initiative, apart from the official government, apart from the official TO, that is to say in Vitez that should have been the Territorial Defence. Until the spring of 1992, that is, I do not know how the Muslim people, the Bosnia people, organised themselves in their defence against the Greater Serbia aggression. So I did not come to the TO staff at my own initiative. It's not that I reported there and tried to give my own contribution, because the situation was such that the shelling of Vitez already started and there were already attacks on Turbe and there was no way out. That was the situation then. And the Greater Serbian aggression was making unbelievable progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, let us speak concretely. During the last six months of 1992, let's go even beyond that, let's say the end of 1992, which units were manning the front in those areas closest to Vitez, let's say in the area of Zenica, which units were manning the front against the Serbs? If you don't know, sir, please just say so. I am asking you this question to see whether you are in any position to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: From mid-1992 until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I know that parts of our units held the frontline against the Serbs above Novi Travnik, towards Bijelo Bucje, towards Komar that is, Kamenjasi, Mravnjaci and Slatka Voda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Which units were involved here, sir?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, at the level of the municipality of Vitez, a battalion was established, up to 300 men it had, I believe, and these men went to the frontline against the Serb aggressor, and they took shifts. Sixty to 100 men would go per shift to fight the frontline against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's take the case of this battalion. Can you describe for us what this battalion was composed of, when it was created, and who was in command of it?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time this battalion belonged to the Tomasevic Brigade and the commander was Boro Malbasic, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that time, again I am referring to the second half of the year 1992, were there any other units than the Croat unit which you mentioned, the Bosnian Croatian units, present at the front?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question. What units?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I asked you, sir, which units were present at the front, and you specified that there was a battalion made up of Bosnian Croats, if I understood you correctly. I would like for you to tell me whether there were other units at that site, other units than the one composed of Bosnian Croats which was also present at that time on the front against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the way it was. At that time, in addition to this unit, I know that there were some kind of units in the form of village patrols. These are these other Croat units, as you call them, that were not attached to the brigade system. This was self-organised people, and they mainly operated at night and guarded their houses, et cetera, and I was one of them. I was on one of these guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I think, perhaps, we are not completely understanding each other. I was requesting to see whether or not there were other units, Muslim units, if there were any, at this frontline in the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I know that the units of the Bosniak army were at the frontline against the Serb aggressors, and I think that they held the frontline above Travnik towards Vlasic. And specifically which units at this moment, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, let us now talk about this village guard which you referred to. Who made up this guard, this village guard?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Neighbours, ordinary peasants in the place where they lived. That is to say that a group of people would organise themselves and protect their houses, the roads leading to them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What was the command of this village guard?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what the situation was like in other places, but I can tell you about what it was like where I was in this village guard. We organised ourselves at our own initiative and we would agree amongst ourselves who would be on duty, when and for how long. So as long as I was there standing guard, no one ever came to see us, either military or civilian authorities. So we were truly self-organised in terms of defending our houses, our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were the village guards in all villages in the area of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't really say. I just know that we organised this village guard in that part of Krusica, and I imagine that the majority of the Croat people was organised in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the end of the year 1992. You stated that at that time, at the invitation of Colonel Blaskic, you went to the headquarters of the operational zone where you were given command of the operations, this in the beginning, or at the end rather, of the month of November, 1992; is that correct? Can we say that the post you received was a post of confidence, a high level one?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't receive command over the operations. I was simply in charge of operational matters, and above me was the chief of staff and above him Blaskic. So I was only in charge of operations in the staff, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I had understood, but perhaps I made an error in thinking that you were in charge of the operations under the authority of Colonel Blaskic at that time. Thank you for specifying that, what your duties were. Were you not also a member of a coordination group for the HVO activities within the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I said in my statement that Colonel Blaskic told me verbally to coordinate the passage of units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian army to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let me then go back to this joint commission between the HVO and the Bosnian army. Can you please, first of all, confirm that you were a member of this coordinating committee representing the HVO and, if so, can you please give us some details about the activities of that commission, that group.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never said that it was a commission which was set up by someone. I only said that I was commanded verbally by Blaskic to coordinate the passage of HVO and the BiH units to the frontline. But I was not a member of any committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Then you did not represent the HVO within a commission composed of members of the HVO and members of the BiH Army, and also members of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right. It was an internal order by Colonel Blaskic to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand you correctly, sir. You never were a member of this commission; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you are aiming at, sir. I have reiterated twice that I was not a member of that commission, but only that I received an oral internal order by Commander Blaskic that I was to coordinate the passage of the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and HVO up to the frontline. I think I have been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, I am sorry. Perhaps you feel you are being clear. I am not sure I myself understand you clearly. Perhaps I am in error. But I would like to know -- what I am interested in is this joint commission made up of representatives of the HVO, members of the BiH Army, and also members of the European Monitoring Mission. I would like to know whether or not you were at one point in time under the orders, of course, of Colonel Blaskic, the representative for the HVO at this commission?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. President, may I produce a document? I have not disclosed this document. I did not think there would be any discussion about this issue. I have not yet disclosed this document to the Defence. It's not truly a problem. I simply wish to show this document to the witness and, perhaps, it's something he's forgotten, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, granted. Do you have photocopies for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, no I do not. I didn't intend on using this document at all. I did not expect to have a discussion on this particular point. I did not anticipate using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radovic. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judge, this way of proceeding has put us in a very unfavourable position. We do not know what this document is and we cannot use the information in this document in our cross-examination. You have decided that the document can be used by the Prosecution in their cross-examination, but when we are examining the witness, we would like to ask that a photocopy of the document be delivered to us before and that we should be given sufficient time to study it. That's all that we are asking at this moment, with reference to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't want to raise any difficulties at all with regard to this issue. We simply wish to take the document back, then, if it's going to cause a problem. I simply wish to have the witness be aware of its contents in order to receive an explanation. Perhaps there is no mystery at all in these answers. Perhaps I am the only one not understanding or perhaps we need further explanations from the witness. But I do not wish to make this into an incident. It does not really justify having all these dealings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you intend to read some passages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I intend to explain to the witness what the content of this document is, what the substance is of this document, and see whether or not this brings up any -- recalls any memories on his part. If not, then I can see right away and then we'll go onto another series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you hear the proposal from the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour. Will the usher please give me the document back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, we are now going back to our question. I have here before me an order signed by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic dated the 15th of February, 1993 at 8.30 p.m. It is stated here that given that Mario Rajic is ill, that he be replaced, rather, in this coordination committee. He should be replaced with Mr. Tomo Vlajic. A copy of this order shall be given to the European Community Monitoring Mission, as well as to the army of BiH, the 3rd Corps, as well as other persons whose names I will not mention now. Now, it is on the basis of this document that I believed, sir, that you were a member of this joint commission, this joint coordination committee.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: What I have just said, Colonel Blaskic told me verbally that I was to coordinate the passage of the units through the checkpoints up to the defence lines. I do not recall that this commission ever met, actually, or ever started working. I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the transcript on line 19.5, I see the name of Tomo Vlajic. That's an error there. It should be Vlajic. Sir, do you recall that this gentleman fell ill at that time and was replaced by another person?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's possible, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief you stated that you left the HVO in mid-March, 1992. You also specified that you were demobilised, and you used the term "demobilised." So using this term, I believe, it will call up something in my mind, it calls up two things in particular -- rather, correction, you made this mention twice. Now, in 1992, at this time -- in mid-March, 1993, pardon me, I stand corrected, 1993, this was not a time period which was particularly calm or peaceful, so why would you have been demobilised at that time?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the period before I was with Colonel Blaskic, I was the head of a car repair shop in Vitez, and it's well-known that Vitezit rented this to UNPROFOR. So all the equipment was transferred to the Vitezit company, and this was a large amount of property which was not under any kind of control, so that the director of the factory requested in writing from Colonel Blaskic that I should be released and returned to the factory in order to supervise the work of that service and the control of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I see. Since you talked about the fact that you were demobilised in March, 1993, are we to understand that before that time you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is how it was: As I said, I arrived in the -- in the staff of the Operative Zone, as it was then called, at the invitation of Blaskic. It was not a mobilisation, it was an invitation to which I responded, and I was appointed, at the order of Colonel Blaskic, to be in charge of operations, and according to Blaskic's decision, I was relieved of that duty at the request of the director of my factory. If I used the word "demobilised," it was probably just a spontaneous slip, but this is how really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, I assure you that you did use the term "demobilised," otherwise, I would not have taken the liberty of using it here again. The Defence counsel that put the question to you, she herself -- or counsel herself used that term. Nonetheless, we do not require any further explanation. Am I to understand from what you've just said, sir, that you had close relations or personal relations, at least, with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know Colonel Blaskic until I was invited to join the staff, I never met him before. And Colonel Blaskic treated every one equally, in a professional manner. It could never be called a close relationship. In any case, it was only a professional relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, I believe during the previous testimony you talked about the Vitez Brigade and the fact that it was divided into two parts. You also stated that initially the brigade in Vitez was made up of 300 men. Now, in this reorganisation of the HVO in Travnik and in Vitez, did this lead to general increase in the number of men?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: The question is not completely clear to me, but this is how it was: I said that the Vitez Brigade had about 300 men at that time, and that this was in late '92 and early '93, and that it was part of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. I think that this kind of organisation reduced the defence ability -- capacity of Vitez and of the brigade Stjepan Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you specify your response by indicating how the number of men changed in the Vitez Brigade? Now we're talking about the first trimester of the 1993.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think that in the first trimester of 1993 the number of members of the brigade increased. I'm referring to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade and later the Vitez Brigade. You know that in early 1993 there was a command to the effect that the Vitez Brigade should be organised, should be set up as a special unit, and that the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade should be split into two brigades, one of which would be the Vitez Brigade and the other one the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You confirm then that the creation of the Vitez Brigade was made up -- created, rather, without giving any men to it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I couldn't have said that, you know. The Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade consisted of units from Vitez and from Novi Travnik, so the command of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade consisted of part of the commanders of Vitez and some of the commanders from Novi Travnik. When the Vitez Brigade was set up a special command for the Vitez Brigade had to be set up, and the number of 300 men had to be organised into a brigade, and this was not done in the first trimester of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, let us pass on now to another question. During your testimony you spoke in great detail about the mobilisation procedure, and it seemed to me that you insisted a great deal about the administrative aspects of this mobilisation procedure, as well as the formalities that were involved and that had to be complied with and in conformity with the law. You talked about a secret mobilisation as well. What is a secret mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: A secret mobilisation? Well, the difference between a public and a secret mobilisation, a public one is announced over the radio, television, the press, and members of units are publicly asked to come to a certain places. A secret mobilisation is when every member receives a personal command to come to the place where they are to assemble.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand you, sir, now. I take it there was no other way of informing someone that they were being called up except by letter? I note, for example, the defence of the Croatian community. Couldn't one use the telephone, for example, or a fax if necessary or other means of communication?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: The HVO could not notify me because I was not mobilised in the HVO, and I was not detailed to the HVO but in the TO. I know how this is done because I was mobilised several times before the war, and I always received a written summons which I had to sign in the presence of a witness, and then I had to show up at the assembly point. So I could not respond to a mobilisation from the HVO because I did not have a role in the HVO at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, witness, you're saying that -- you stated how the mobilisation was organised before the war but you do not know what the procedure was within the HVO during the war.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's quite clear from the document you gave me. This shows what the mobilisation of 16th April of 1993 was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, I am not referring to a document. I want to be very clear. This is a remark that you made, that you talked about the mobilisation procedure before the war and not within HVO during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to submit document 343 to the witness. This is a document which was already -- it's already been shown during the examination-in-chief. Mr. President, when this document was shown to the witness during the examination-in-chief, Counsellor Radovic spoke of the difficulty in reading the document. Indeed, that is true. There is a word on this order which I have difficulty reading. In fact, it could even lead to a misunderstanding. I wish to put this -- put the original document to this Tribunal. I do not wish to disclose it as an exhibit -- rather, to submit it as an exhibit, but we simply wish to show it to the bench and also to the Defence to remove all doubt about any confusion that might be in reading in document. Perhaps the usher may come forward and, first of all, show this document to Your Honours, and then after that to the members of the Defence. Mr. President, with the permission of this Tribunal, may I request members of the Defence whether we may come to an agreement that the word that was causing the problem is indeed "army" and not "non-army?" Correction, "armed" and "not armed."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After we have seen the original document we can agree that it says "armed." "Armed" members of the Croatian people should be included in the units, because the photocopy was not clear, but now we see the original document and the English translation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, in this document it's indicated, under the signature of Colonel Blaskic, dated of the 16th -- 15th -- 16th of January, 1993, that at the highest level within the HVO all combat units of the HVO must be at maximum alert, and that all armed members of the Croatian people must be included in the HVO training, or formations, rather, and there should be no further dispute about the English translation of this order from Colonel Blaskic. In response to the question put to you by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac about the administrative capacity of Colonel Blaskic to order the mobilisation, the question is as follows: Why ask Colonel Blaskic to give this order and what, to your knowledge, were the effects of such an order?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to intervene and say that it is not mentioned anywhere here that all the armed members of the Croatian people have to be included in the HVO. So I don't know whether this is a slip of the tongue. It means -- it refers only to inclusion in the units. That's what I wanted to say, because the Prosecutor said that they all had to be included in the HVO and this is not evident from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to rephrase my question in the following way: Sir, in this order from Colonel Blaskic which was shown to you during the examination-in-chief, it is ordered by the person signing this document, that is to say, Colonel Blaskic, that one must raise the combat readiness of HVO formations to the highest level, that all HVO formations are to be at a maximum state of readiness and that all armed members of the Croatian people are to be included in the HVO formations. When this document was shown to you during the examination-in-chief, you stated that given your understanding of the administrative rules, that the mobilisations did not come under the power of Colonel Blaskic. I would like now for you to respond to a number of questions. First of all, why would Colonel Blaskic give this order of 16th January, 1993; and second, second question, if you would like to answer it: What were the actual concrete or specific effects of this order?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if we are referring to armed members, I understood that this was to be a mobilisation of the unarmed Croatian people. Colonel Blaskic was not authorised to give this order, and I still say that under the conditions prevailing at that time it was the civilian government that was authorised to issue this order. What Colonel Blaskic meant, I assume, was that he was referring to people who are on leave, who were perhaps on sick leave and who were members of the units to which the order refers. Why the combat readiness was raised, well, this, as you probably know, happened quite often, because every time something happened in the area of responsibility in an operations area, combat readiness was raised to train the army because of the situation and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, today we know that Colonel Blaskic was referring to the armed members of the Croatian people. Who was he referring to, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that he was probably referring to those people who were at home, on leave, and who at that time were not active in the units. So they were on leave, free. Well, that means, actually, the units should being activated in their entirety. That is to say that a soldier cannot be active around the clock, 24 hours a day. We did not live in barracks, we lived at home. That is to say that those who were off then and who were members of the Vitez Brigade were supposed to report to their units, and that is to say that combat readiness was to be raised to a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you were questioned about the participation of Croatian citizens in the war against the Serbs, you stated -- you made very severe comments about the role of the civilians at the front, stating that they went to the front in a way to -- rather, they avoided going to the front in order to save their lives. In that way, participation in the effort were quite low. Do you feel, perhaps, this is being -- you're being very severe about the role played by your fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you understood me correctly when we were discussing this, I said that the citizens of Vitez who were taken to the frontline on the 16th of April, I said that they were unprepared, that they were unarmed. I was not -- I was quite tolerant in this respect. So I'm not talking about units that went to the frontline against the Serbs, I'm talking about units that were -- not units but people who were called on the morning of the 16th of April, and later on until the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were talking about people who were engaged in which battle in April?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not talking about a battle in April, I was talking about people who were called up all over town and taken to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You also underlined the importance of military training. Can you please specify whether it was possible for a person to use an infantry weapon, for example, a pistol or an automatic rifle, for example, without having received any type of military training?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because there were persons who had rifles and pistols and who were not trained to do so, we had a lot of wounds that were self-inflicted, a lot of people who were killing themselves and a great many other accidents of this nature. And there were some people who never held a rifle in their hands before, and who were taken to the frontline with a rifle in their hands. I'm not only talking about individual cases, I think that one could say that this was the majority of the cases involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is quite simple. Can one use an automatic weapon, let's say like an AK-47, without having received training in firing?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: In order to be able to use it, in order to be able to shoot, it is sufficient to train a person for half an hour, for example, just to be able to trigger it. However, to use it properly, to use it effectively, one needs training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 16th of April, 1993, where were you located?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1994 I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: 1993, sir. I'm referring to 1993. 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, 1993. '93? Oh, yes, yes, I was at home. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you mean in your house in your village?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. At my family home -- my family house in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You didn't go to work on that day in the factory in Vitezit?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No. On the 15th I was at the Vitezit factory, but on the morning of the 16th, around 6.00 in the morning, I was awakened by a detonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And why did you not go to work on the 16th of April, 1993? Why did you remain at home?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, naturally there was terrible shelling and I didn't feel safe going to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know what transpired in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I found out about that only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you specify what you learned and when you learned it?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think immediately the next day I learned that there was a big conflict in Ahmici. This was hearsay. Villagers were telling one another about it, so I heard about it in the basement of my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you please specify what you learned.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I learned that a violent conflict took place where many persons lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you told what type of victims they were at that time?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. I was told that most of the victims were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That I did not know whether they were civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And after the month of April, 1993, did you return to a position of authority within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: A position of authority? Four days after the war broke out, that is to say on the 20th of April, 1993, I was escorted by a military policeman and taken to the headquarters of the Vitez Brigade, and I was appointed adviser for operations and teaching affairs. So I really don't see where there is authority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Didn't you return to the position within the joint commission representing the HVO in this joint committee with the BiH Army together with representatives from the European Monitoring Mission and also the UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I returned to the job of adviser for operations and teaching affairs in the Vitez Brigade. That was my military assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, I understood your answer, however, I would like to request a specific answer from you. Is it true that you resumed duties within a coordination committee, a joint commission, bringing together members of the Bosnian army and the HVO and made up also of members of UNPROFOR and the European Monitoring Commission?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: On several occasions I attended such meetings at UNPROFOR premises, but I do not recall any documents appointing me as member of that commission. At any rate, I did not go back to the operative zone to Colonel Blaskic. I was appointed in the Vitez Brigade as adviser for operations in teaching affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well. We'll now take a 30-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Is Counsel Radovic going to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I will conduct part of the examination referring to the organisation of the Territorial Defence and questions will be put by my colleague, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need to introduce myself. Could you please tell me, since I see that there are some points that are not clear, when people who had served their regular service in the JNA came back, were they all detailed to units of the Territorial Defence or were some of them put in other JNA units, mobile JNA units? Could you please answer clearly and press the button for the microphone. You have to have a red light.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. After serving the army term, some were called up into TO units, some into mobile units, and some were not assigned to any units at.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So they were not assigned to any units?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the military distribution in the JNA, some persons who held key positions in companies which were important for the JNA war effort, could they be assigned to stay in their companies?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct. Certain managers, services were organised as a wartime production.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Persons assigned to the so-called military production, did such people have any connections or obligation to serve in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were such people called to come to exercises of the TO?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When talking about your military training, you said that you had completed the course for a battalion commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What was the corresponding rank in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that would be Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what a battalion consisted of in the JNA, because you were asked about this previously, but we should clarify some points, because you and I understand it, but it needs to be clarified. So an infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: An infantry battalion, in principle, had a staff with units, it had three infantry companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the terminology of the former JNA, so we will use the word for company that was used in the JNA. What else was there?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Battalion also had support battery, an artillery battery, and then it had a logistics company, it had a communications department in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the Territorial Defence in Vitez was a strengthened battalion. What did the strengthening consist of?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Every company had the support of accompanying artillery pieces, so there were recoilless guns, mortars and machine guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many artillery pieces would belong to a reinforced company?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: There would be three machine guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many mortars?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Our unit had a mortar platoon, 22 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And how many recoilless guns?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were two recoilless guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the Territorial Defence, as it was envisaged by the JNA was functioning, was that Territorial Defence organised along a single nationality principle or were there people of various nationalities?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time the Territorial Defence was organised regardless of national affiliation and it reflected more or less the structure of the population, the make-up of the population in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When mobilisation for the Territorial Defence was planned, did the latter Territorial Defence have an assembly point?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was a part of the village of Gacice, Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So all the members of the Territorial Defence that the JNA intended to mobilise into the TO through the then secretariat for All People's Defence would receive draft notes and they would have to assemble at a certain place?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct, on the date that was stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Every lower level unit had its own assembly point, so every company had its own assembly point. The equipment would be brought to the assembly point in the meantime, and the files from the People's Defence Secretariat would be brought there, and the commander would then set up his unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the weapons of the TO, where were they stored before this was centralised?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the Territorial Defence depots which were close to the Vitez municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was that under military or civilian administration, if we consider the TO was civilian?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was under civilian administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did it remain like this until the end or did the JNA remove the weapons before these events?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that while I was at the factory the weapons that we had to defend the factory had to be moved to the JNA depot, so that all of the weapons were placed in the JNA depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said something about using an automatic rifle in answer to a question by the Prosecution, and you said that anyone could use one because all you had to do was put the bullet in and then press the trigger.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So tell us, before a previous learning about the characteristics, the combat characteristics of this gun, is it possible to use it, because you know that when you shoot this the barrel points upwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So a person who is not familiar with this characteristic of an automatic rifle, can they use it efficiently, or would they be shooting into the air?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Anyone who is not trained to use an automatic rifle cannot use it efficiently and hit the target, because you know that the bullets go up and to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Another question about whether automatic rifles can be used without training. Do such guns have to be cleaned?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the rifle has to be cleaned several times a day in order to be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: To clean this rifle, do you have to take it apart before you begin cleaning it, and then do you have to reassemble it after cleaning?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can this be done by a person who has not practised doing it before?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have completed my part of the cross-examination. My colleague will go on now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Rajic, can you say something else that my colleague forgot to ask. How many people were included in the TO in the Vitez municipality? What was the number of people involved?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but it might have been about 600 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the population of the Vitez municipality, the number of members of the Territorial Defence refers to the entire municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this refers to the TO and the units connected to the Vitez TO. There were about 23.000 inhabitants at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So only a limited number of inhabitants were included in the TO units?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were in the active reserves of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: With reference to your response to the Prosecutor's question as to the positions of the HVO and the army of BiH toward the Serbs, you spoke of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the HVO was involved in the defence of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was the part of the HVO or the Vitez Brigade or the Stjepan Tomasevic at that time involved? Do you know whether the men went there?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: A question related to the establishing of the Vitez Brigade. You said that decision had been made in January, '93 that the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade should be split into two parts and that one part should, or rather that the second battalion should become or join the Vitez Brigade. What did this mean, in fact, with reference to the number of men? Did this have any effect or was it simply a movement?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct. The existing battalion, with part of the command of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, those who were from Vitez were simply moved to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this means that only the command crossed over to the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Part of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was part of the command before?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the hotel in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the only change that came about with the establishing of the Vitez Brigade was to move the command post, in a manner of speaking, and to set up a command in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: As regards the number of men, there were no changes?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the reason for this? Why was this done?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it proved to be inefficient to have a part of the Vitez command in Novi Travnik and for the army to be linked organisationally to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, and it became evident that Vitez had, in fact, remained without its own defence and its own command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you were still in the operational zone in March, '93?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, up to mid March.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The number of men in the Vitez Brigade was about 300?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the registrar to show the witness 5335 -- Exhibit P335. Mr. Rajic, you've already seen this document. You saw it during the examination-in-chief, and you see that it pertains to mobilisation and that it is the report on mobilisation between the 16th to the 28th of April, 1994. Do you know who was mobilised on the 16th out of these men?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean by name?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, I can. I can say for sure that I know that some of these people were mobilised on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were mobilised on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you say at which rate the mobilisation progressed in terms of this particular interval between the 16th and the 28th?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say which -- what the exact tempo was. Some people were taken to the frontline and then taken back, and then some people were taken to the frontline again. So it's very difficult to say which number of people were taken to the frontline at a given point in time, you see. That is why the same names reappear at several different places in this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So according to this list we cannot say who was mobilised when, except in the cases that you are aware of on a personal level.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can one tell, on the basis of this list, which frontlines these men went to?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us one more thing, in relation to Kruscica, you told us you lived there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I lived in the lower part of Kruscica. That is to say, the entrance to Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is actually a part of Vitez; right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It's a suburb; right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In that part, can you say where the village of Kruscica begins? Did you border on the village of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the village of Kruscica begins perhaps half a kilometre away from my house, towards Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, where was the defence line placed in relation to Kruscica? I mean, when the war operations started and during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in relation to my house, about 2 or 300 kilometres away from my house. Up to 500 metres away from my house towards the village of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That was the defence line that was placed at the very outbreak of the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And that part, 500 metres away from your house, that is where Muslim-held territory started, that is BH army-held territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us also, in relation to Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, where do you know them from? Is this a personal thing?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mentioned it last time. I've known Zoran for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where from?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the factory. We worked together. We worked for the same company. In quite a few situations we were compelled to co-operate due to our actual work, because he was employed in the transport department and, therefore, we co-operated at work. Then on the other hand, personally, we knew each other for years through folklore, and it is from those days that I knew Mirjan too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you do not know about them -- or, rather, you are not aware of their military involvement in any way?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have any military co-operation with either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no questions from the Court. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released? Mr. Rajic, thank you for giving evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether the next witness is going to enjoy protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Matic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder if Mr. Matic could be called in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Matic. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us your name and surname for the purposes of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Andelko (sic) Matic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Again, there is a mistake. In the transcript it says "Andelko" with an "O" at the end and that is a man's name. So it should be corrected as an "A" at the end, "Andelka." So your name is Andelka Matic. Where were you born and when?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: I was born on the 16th of October, 1951 in the village of Gacice, and I'm a housewife.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And could we see Prosecutor's Exhibit number 1? Mrs. Matic, can you tell us how far away the village of Gacice is from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: About a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You're going to show it to us on the map. That is to say, where the village is. Could you please tell us where it is?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Can I take off my headphones, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Right. Tell us, what was the ethnic composition of the village?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: The ethnic composition in the village of Gacice was about half/half. Half Croat, half Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what was the population of Gacice in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure, but I think about 200 Croats and 200 Muslims respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what was the layout of the houses in the village? Were Muslim houses concentrated in a certain part of the village and Croatian houses in another part of the village?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Well, part of the village that we call the centre of the village was purely Muslim, and the other part is mixed Croat and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In 1992, were village guards organised by Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes. When the war with the Serbs broke out, then the Muslims and the Croats agreed to stand guard duty in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And this guard duty, was it a joint thing throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: No. No. There was joint guard duty at the end of October, and then the Muslims stole two guns, two cannons, they simply drove them away, and then this joint guard duty was split up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: These two guns, where were they and how come? How did they reach Gacice?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: These guns were not in the village, they were below the village, below our cemetery and the Muslims' cemetery. The guns belonged to the enterprise. These were anti-aircraft guns, and as Serbian aircraft were flying over our area they were used for defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So actually this was part of the anit-aircraft defence of the SPS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And after these guns disappeared the guard split up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes, the guard split up. There were two Croat men and two Muslim men patrolling the village again, but not together but separately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This guard duty in the village, who did it involve? Who actually stood guard, younger people, elderly people?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Well, sometimes it was younger people, sometimes it was older people. They took shifts so that it wouldn't be too hard for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did people go out to do their guard duty armed?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they would carry a weapon, and sometimes the person who would be taking over would not have a weapon, and then the person who he was replacing would give him his weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see Muslims carrying weapons when they went out for guard duty?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes. They always said that they would take hunting guns out but they actually had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they sometimes go out in uniforms? Did they have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had uniforms with TO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms are these, what colour?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Well, bluish, bluish. Single coloured bluish uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And after the guard duty split up, were there any incidents in the village, was there any trouble?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: No. No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And were there any incidents whatsoever in this village, apart from the fact that these guns were driven away?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 16th of April, 1993, where were you and what happened?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: On the 16th of April I was at home. On the 16th of April shooting started in the neighbouring villages, and we could hear it well, particularly from Veceriska because it is on the other side of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you heard shooting in Veceriska. Did you hear anything from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes, from the direction of Vitez and Kruscica, but mostly from Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what was going on in the village? Did war operations start in the village itself?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: No. People were quite frightened. Both peoples were frightened. Then the Croats elected one man and then the Muslims did the same thing, and this representative of the Croat people of the village went to negotiate with the Muslim representative.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who were these men?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: The Croat was Anto Krizanovic, and the Muslim was Kadir Hrustic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what did they negotiate about? What did each side ask for?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Well, I heard that the negotiations were related to the handover of weapons, but that is what each side requested of the other but they could not reach agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know how long this went on, these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And during those two or three days in Gacice nothing happened?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did anybody leave Gacice at that time?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: At that time nobody left the village. There were some people that did not return, people who had left because of the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were they Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Both Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So for how long did this go on? How long did it remain peaceful in Gacice?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Until the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what happened on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: On the 20th of April shooting started in our village too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When? At what time?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Around 7.00 two or three stronger detonations were heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: After that, shooting started all over. There were bullets flying all over, from rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: At that time I was in my house, and I spent part of this time in the basement when there was a lot of shooting. Then when it would subside a bit then I would go up to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: I saw three men in uniform, in camouflage uniforms. They were carrying an orange canister. They were torching my brothers-in-law's houses, Fabjan Matic, Ivo Matic, Marko Matic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Whose soldiers were they?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: They were Muslim soldiers, but as they walked in front of my house along the road, I saw the chequerboard sign on their caps. That is to say that they were masked. When they reached my house, shooting stopped from the Muslim part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who were these people? Were they Muslims from the village?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Two were the sons of Ramulj Handija and one was the son of Avdo Herceg.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You recognised them?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you say what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: They -- at the crossroads in front of my house they crossed over to the Muslim side, went to the village and the fighting went on again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did the fighting last?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: The shooting lasted until 4.00 or 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that who retreated from the village?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: After that, when the shooting started, I saw a group of Muslims with a white flag beside my house, and I heard that a group had come out at the bottom of the village but I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which of these two groups were Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: No, they were Muslim civilians, women, children, elderly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where did the soldiers go?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: The soldiers went above the village, through the woods, in the direction of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the soldiers left the village?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did -- were the soldiers disarmed or was anything done to them?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: No. A corridor was left open for them to leave and no weapons were taken from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened to the civilians in the village?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Well, the civilians, as I heard, were taken to Vitez, to the town, but they were brought back quickly and they settled in the lower part of the village, in the direction of Vitez, in several Muslim houses where they would spend the night, and they were always guarded by two Croats from the village overnight. In the morning they would go back to their homes and go about their everyday business.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And how long did this situation last?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Well, about 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened after that? Did they leave Gacice?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: After 15 days, in the evening, as they were in a few houses at the bottom of the village, I heard that some trucks had come to pick them up and that they had left in the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you saw that several houses were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Those were Croatian houses in the part of the village where you were?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were any other Croatian houses set on fire?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes. Two other Croatian buildings were set on fire. That was at the other end of the village. Those were houses belonging to my brother, but about ten Muslim houses were burnt as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were the houses burnt during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether -- or what happened to the other Muslim houses? Were they destroyed later or did they remain the way they were?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: After that Croatian refugees arrived from the area of Zenica. They moved into the Muslim houses. The houses remained intact, except that an old house belonging to Cerpic, which had been hit by a shell, started caving in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were the houses repaired?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes, all the houses were repaired and the Muslims came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that the Muslim army retreated through the woods in the direction of Kruscica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Andelka Matic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
